overview: The Miami, or Myaamia, are a Great Lakes people whose farming villages and river connections supported wide regional influence. The broad Myaamia and narrower Miami outlines are approximations. A separate Oklahoma outline dated 1492 is anachronistic: Miami settlement there followed nineteenth-century removals. Miami communities continue in Oklahoma, Indiana and beyond.

periods.title: Homelands and regional power
periods.summary: Miami villages linked farming country and waterways; leaders later helped organize resistance to United States expansion.

periods.title: Treaties and shrinking landholdings
periods.summary: Land cessions and mounting pressure culminated in forced removal of many Miami families.

periods.title: Separation and further displacement
periods.summary: Removed families rebuilt in Kansas, then faced another move toward Indian Territory; others remained in Indiana.

periods.title: Continuing communities and renewal
periods.summary: The Oklahoma and Indiana communities continued, and language programs now connect people across dispersed homes.

sections.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation

items.text: Miami villages stood near rivers that connected settlements through canoe travel. The Indiana community’s history places their homeland across parts of present-day Indiana, Ohio, Illinois and Michigan. Hunting, fishing and cultivation worked together in a landscape where water routes could link relatives and trading partners.

Miami white flour corn drew an early eighteenth-century observer’s attention for its fine husks and pale flour. Historian Cameron Shriver follows this crop through later sources, including twentieth-century Miami farmers. Corn was both a lasting food tradition and an agricultural achievement maintained through enormous political change.

In a 2023 account, weaver Jared Nally describes harvesting inner bark from trees such as basswood and gathering other plant fibers later in the year. Separating usable fibers and rolling or spinning thread could take as long as weaving itself. A finished textile contains a great deal of work that is easy not to see.

The winter game snowsnake sends a length of wood sliding through snow. Players try to make it travel farther and straighter than an opponent’s throw. Myaamia community programs have been reviving the game: snow becomes a playing surface, and the snake is reassuringly wooden.

Lacrosse remains an opportunity to meet relatives and neighbors as well as compete. A 2022 community account describes an annual Myaamia game with Seneca-Cayuga participants, including youth camps. It also distinguishes older games from newer adaptations that introduce Myaamia language into familiar card games.

In 2024, Myaamia sugar camps operated in Ohio, Indiana and Oklahoma. Sap was boiled down into syrup or sugar; a typical maple yield required about 40 gallons of sap for one gallon of syrup. Oklahoma participants also tapped black walnut because local sugar maples were scarce. Breakfast sweetness required buckets of effort.

Miami leader Little Turtle helped lead a Native coalition that defeated United States forces in 1790 and 1791. Before the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794, he urged peace. These changing decisions belonged to a wider struggle over homelands involving several allied peoples, rather than one isolated Miami army.

The Treaty of Greenville in 1795 required extensive land cessions. Further treaties narrowed Miami control over their homeland, and an 1840 agreement called for removal beyond the Mississippi. Treaty dates mark government decisions; the forced journey itself came later.

On October 11, 1846, five canal boats carrying Miami people reached Cincinnati. There they were forced aboard the steamboat Colorado to continue west along the Ohio River. A university archival exhibit places this transfer within the removal journey, revealing how ordinary transport networks became instruments of forced displacement.

Other Miami families secured permission to stay in Indiana. Their descendants form the Miami Nation of Indiana, with continuing government, cultural programs and relationships to western Miami relatives. Its own history distinguishes that community’s existence from its lack of federal recognition as a sovereign tribal nation today.

The western Miami faced another move after an 1867 treaty, with migration from Kansas into present-day Oklahoma in the late 1860s and 1870s. The Miami Tribe of Oklahoma established its government there. That sequence explains why an Oklahoma polygon cannot accurately represent Miami territory in 1492.

Language revitalization draws on documents spanning the late 1600s through the 1960s. A Myaamia Center report explains how researchers analyze old records, compare forms and develop resources for present-day use. The work connects archival scholarship with families learning words together; it is a gradual effort across generations.

A short modern writing sample is “Tipeewe neeyolaani”, translated as “It is good to see you.” Miami University’s tribal-relations page prints both forms in its Myaamia teaching list. The greeting follows contemporary community teaching spelling.

During 2023 summer programs, children made miniature lodges with coverings that represented elm bark and cattail mats. They also practiced kinship words on family trees, while older participants made films and mentored younger learners. Model building helped connect household history, language and living family relationships.

ending.text: The imported map cutoffs are not the end of Miami history. Removal created separated communities without ending Miami identity. The Oklahoma Tribe and Indiana community continue, while research and family learning help carry Myaamia language into daily life.
